nodes.label: Arab conquest
nodes.full: The Arab victories of 636–642 bring the Sasanian cane lands of the Sawad and Khuzestan under Muslim rule; the legend that the conquerors then carried cane west has no established basis.

nodes.label: Umar’s cane tax
nodes.full: Umar’s governor taxes cane at 6 dirhams a jarib against 4 for wheat in the conquered Sawad (637), implying cane grown for sugar.

nodes.label: Iraq’s cane
nodes.full: In the tenth century no village in Iraq is without cane, with Sinjar the probable northern limit.

nodes.label: Persia’s provinces
nodes.full: Ahwaz, Jubba and Sus, Fars and Sijistan are Persia’s sugar provinces; Askar Mukram supplies ‘the whole world’.

nodes.label: Sugar in kind
nodes.full: Ahwaz and Sijistan pay 30,000 and 20,000 ratl of sugar in kind under Harun al-Rashid.

nodes.label: Mutanabbi
nodes.full: Al-Mutanabbi praises the hard sugar crystal of Ahwaz.

nodes.label: Syrian cane
nodes.full: Cane in Syria cannot be traced before the tenth century; Tripoli is the first district recorded.

nodes.label: Crete and Sicily
nodes.full: Andalusian Arabs take Crete and the Aghlabids take Sicily in the ninth century.

nodes.label: Sicily’s cane
nodes.full: Persian cane grows in the marshes near Palermo; the export claims are disputed.

nodes.label: Magadha mission
nodes.full: Magadha’s envoy and Wang Xuance’s mission of 647–648: two shi mi artisans and eight monks come to China and make shi mi at Yuezhou.

nodes.label: Tang tribute
nodes.full: Tang areas send cane or sugar to court as tribute, some from Buddhist monasteries, Yuezhou among them.

nodes.label: Dunhuang MS
nodes.full: The Dunhuang fragment describes the Indian crushing and boiling method — the earliest substantial account of sugar-making in China.

nodes.label: Monk Zou
nodes.full: A Tang legend credits a monk in Sichuan with teaching the crystallisation of sugar.

nodes.label: Ibn Masawayh
nodes.full: Ibn Masawayh classes sugar as hot and moist in the humoral scheme.

nodes.label: Hunayn’s Dioscorides
nodes.full: Hunayn’s school translates Dioscorides into Arabic; the quoted version turns ‘Arabia Felix’ into ‘Maghrib’.

nodes.label: al-Razi
nodes.full: Al-Razi writes on the qualities of sugar and the kinds of white sugar.

edges: After the conquest of the Sawad, Umar’s governor surveys the fields and fixes the land-tax rates, including 6 dirhams a jarib for sugarcane.
Sato reads the high cane rate as proof that sugar-making cane grew in Lower Iraq before the conquest; the geographers’ tenth-century Iraq is the later phase of that cane.
Under Harun al-Rashid, Ahwaz pays 30,000 ratl of sugar and Sijistan 20,000 ratl of white sugar in kind.
Al-Mutanabbi’s verse is in praise of the hard sugar crystal made at Ahwaz, the centre of Persian sugar.
Sato traces sugarcane expansion from Iran into Iraq along the Tigris and Euphrates plains, with Iraq’s cane centred on the Sawad.
Sato speculates that cane came from Iraq to southern Syria before the tenth century and then spread to other Syrian districts.
Sato says Arab-Muslim culture permeated the conquered islands with sugar production an important example, though Arabic sources on island cane are few.
Needham: the Xu gaoseng zhuan has the Magadha artisans make shi mi at Yuezhou with imperial approval, and Yuezhou appears among the Tang tribute producers.
Needham reads the Dunhuang fragment as light on the transmission of sugar technology from India to China via Buddhist monks in the Tang.
Mazumdar notes that a Buddhist monk in Sichuan may indeed have known how to make refined sugar, as the legend of Zou says.
Ibn Masawayh worked in the same translation movement as Hunayn, in the House of Wisdom, and both pass Greek knowledge of sugar into the humoral framework of Arabic medicine.
Al-Razi’s account of sugar’s qualities uses the same hot-and-cold humoral scheme that Ibn Masawayh applied to sugar a generation earlier.
